source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2010_CirrhosisMA.pdf, pp. 437–445 (all nine pages, including references); Table 1, Figure 1, Figure 2 and Table 2 checked on rendered pages 440–442, paragraph breaks on pp. 437–438

claims.overstatement: None for this source. The claim says 'is associated with' where the paper speaks of alcohol's causal impact and effect. The authors' public-health remark that up to two drinks a day may not raise morbidity (p. 442) is rightly not carried into the claim; 'at up to about two drinks a day' in the claim describes findings, not advice.
claims.note: Every Rehm 2010 number in the statement and magnitude matches Table 2 (p. 442) and the continuous-model and I² values on p. 441, checked on the rendered pages; 17 studies, published 1980–2003, and 3384 cases match p. 440 and Table 1 (case and sample sums recomputed from Table 1: 3384 and 1,477,887, same). '>60 g = more than five drinks' agrees with the paper's 12-g drink (pp. 438–439). Points the claim could add or adjust: (1) the 'diagnosed cirrhosis' (morbidity) estimates rest on at most six studies, four Italian (three of them case–control) and two Danish cohorts (editors' count from Table 1), and Table 2 gives no number of studies or cases per cell; (2) this paper does not describe its case–control studies as hospital-based, and its cohorts include an occupational one (male Japanese physicians, ref. 32), so 'general-population cohorts' fits loosely; (3) the statement's low-intake summary leaves out men's mortality studies (1.0, 0.6–1.6, at up to 12 g; 1.6, 1.4–2.0, at 12–24 g), which the magnitude gives; (4) the correction of current-abstainer reference groups is described (p. 439) but its size is not reported here; (5) 'share six studies' and the factor 1.24 cannot be checked from this source (its 17 studies are listed in Table 1).

anchors.locator: Results › Characteristics of the included studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Figure 1
anchors.extracted: 17 studies included (Figure 1: 3238 records, 167 after abstract screening, 58 read in full, 41 excluded; 14 cohort and 3 case–control; end-point mortality 11, morbidity 4, both 2). Table 1: published 1980 (Blackwelder) to 2003 (Klatsky); USA 9, Italy 4, Denmark 2, China 1, Japan 1; the 3 case–control studies are Italian (Corrao 1991, 1993, 1997), setting not described. 7 studies reported women and men separately, 2 women only, 5 men only, 3 undifferentiated; 12 datasets for women, 15 for men; 1,477,887 people and 3384 cases. Studies with a morbidity end-point: at most 6 (4 Italian, 2 Danish cohorts; editors' count).

anchors.locator: Methods › Data extraction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Standardisation of alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Where a study gave RRs only against current abstainers, RR and CI were adjusted to a lifetime-abstainer reference using a pooled RR for former drinkers against lifetime abstainers and an estimated ratio of former drinkers to lifetime abstainers (to remove the sick-quitter effect); size of the corrections not reported. Results for both sexes combined were entered for both sexes, and combined mortality-and-morbidity results for both end-points. Intake converted to grams a day with the country's standard drink (12 g otherwise), category midpoints used, open top category set at lower bound plus 75% of the previous category's width.

anchors.locator: Results › Dose–response meta-analyses and potential threshold effects, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Figure 2
anchors.extracted: Continuous (fractional-polynomial) models: best power 0.5 for women, linear for men; heterogeneity remained (women Q = 200.59, I² 72%, 95% CI 63–78%; men Q = 305.22, I² 78%, 72–82%). Dose × end-point interaction significant (women χ² 7.89, 1 d.f., P = 0.005; men 17.06, P ≤ 0.001). Risk rose continuously with intake in both sexes and both end-points, more steeply for mortality. Against women lifetime abstainers: mortality RR 4.9 (4.0–6.2) at 24 g a day and 12.5 (8.8–17.7) at 60 g; morbidity 3.2 (2.6–3.9) and 6.2 (4.4–8.7); men a similar, weaker pattern (curves only).

anchors.locator: Table 2 (random-effects categorical models by sex and end-point)
Results › Dose–response meta-analyses and potential threshold effects, 6th paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Exceptions to the gradient: women's morbidity at one to two drinks a day (>12–24 g) RR 1.0 (0.5–1.9), P = 0.981, with two to three drinks (>24–36 g) the lowest significantly raised category, 2.4 (1.8–3.2), P ≤ 0.001; a similar threshold in men's mortality studies (Table 2: 1.0 at >0–12 g, P = 0.991, then 1.6, 1.4–2.0); men in morbidity studies drinking one to two drinks a day had a lower risk than lifetime abstainers, 0.3 (0.2–0.4) (Table 2 also 0.3, 0.1–0.9, at >0–12 and 0.7, 0.5–1.0, at >24–36). Women's mortality raised from the lowest category (1.9, 1.1–3.1, P = 0.013).

Authors: in the categorical analysis up to two drinks a day was not significantly associated with cirrhosis morbidity in either sex, every category above two drinks (women) or three drinks (men) was; in women's mortality studies risk was raised from one drink a day, consistent with no threshold; a very low threshold in men could not be ruled out. They attribute the lack of difference at up to 12 g to light occasional drinkers being counted as drinkers and conclude the results point to a threshold for morbidity but not for mortality.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 1st to 5th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Publication-bias tests not significant (pp. 440–441: women Begg P = 0.837, Egger P = 0.215; men 0.767 and 0.196). Only average volume analysed; for cohorts, baseline drinking assumed to stand for drinking over time; binge drinking and beverage type could not be analysed for lack of data. Few studies of light to moderate drinking with morbidity as end-point; the apparent protective effect of up to two standard drinks a day has no known biological pathway; data with former drinking assessed separately from lifetime abstention needed.

claims.overstatement: On one point the claim understates this source (see note). Otherwise careful: it says 'relative risks', sets each against same-sex abstainers and says a larger ratio does not mean more women than men get cirrhosis, which is more cautious than the paper's abstract (a 'higher risk' in women than in men).
claims.note: All Rehm 2010 figures in the statement and magnitude match Table 2 and p. 441 (checked on the rendered page): 14.7 (11.0–19.6) against 7.0 (5.8–8.5); 5.9 (3.7–9.3) against 2.3 (1.7–3.2); 1.9 (1.4–2.6) against 2.0 (1.5–2.7) at >36–48 g morbidity; women's continuous values 4.9, 12.5, 3.2, 6.2. 'No source tested the sex difference' holds for this paper (sexes analysed separately, p. 440), and 'three studies counted for both sexes' is right (pp. 439–440). Not supported: 'The intervals overlap at most levels'. In this paper the women's and men's 95% CIs overlap in only 4 of 12 cells, and in none of the five mortality levels above 12 g a day (anchor 2; editors' comparison, recomputed). Non-overlap is not a formal test, and the two sexes' estimates share studies, but as written the sentence understates the separation in the earlier meta-analysis. Suggest: in the earlier meta-analysis the intervals did not overlap at most levels; in the newer one and in the Danish cohort they overlapped (in Askgaard, at both levels). '2.0 against 1.9' is the only cell in this paper where the men's figure is higher.

anchors.locator: Results › Dose–response meta-analyses and potential threshold effects, 5th paragraph (right column); Table 2 (p. 442)
anchors.extracted: Women had higher RRs than men at the same intake in both mortality and morbidity studies: at five drinks a day (>48–60 g) mortality 14.7 (11.0–19.6) in women against 7.0 (5.8–8.5) in men; morbidity 5.9 (3.7–9.3) against 2.3 (1.7–3.2), the sex difference less marked in morbidity studies. Each sex is compared with lifetime abstainers of that sex (Table 2 footnotes b, c); one drink = 12 g.

anchors.locator: Table 2, women's rows against men's rows
anchors.extracted: 95% CIs of women and men compared cell by cell (editors' comparison): no overlap at mortality >12–24 (4.5–6.9 vs 1.4–2.0), >24–36 (6.3–9.5 vs 2.3–3.4), >36–48 (7.5–13.5 vs 4.5–7.0), >48–60 (11.0–19.6 vs 5.8–8.5) and >60 (17.2–30.1 vs 11.7–16.7), or at morbidity >12–24 (0.5–1.9 vs 0.2–0.4), >24–36 (1.8–3.2 vs 0.5–1.0) and >48–60 (3.7–9.3 vs 1.7–3.2); overlap only at mortality >0–12 and morbidity >0–12, >36–48 and >60 (4 of 12). Men higher only at morbidity >36–48 (2.0 vs 1.9). No formal test of a sex difference reported.

anchors.locator: Methods › Data extraction, 2nd paragraph; Results › Characteristics of the included studies, 1st paragraph (p. 440); Results › Dose–response meta-analyses, 7th paragraph (p. 442)
anchors.extracted: Three studies without results by sex (refs 30, 36, 40) were entered in both the women's and the men's datasets; 7 studies gave results for both sexes, 2 women only, 5 men only (12 datasets for women, 15 for men), so the two sexes' estimates are not independent. A sensitivity analysis restricted to studies with sex- and end-point-specific results gave a very similar pattern; the authors note that adding undifferentiated studies to both sexes attenuates the differences.

anchors.locator: Results › Dose–response meta-analyses and potential threshold effects, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2
anchors.extracted: Continuous model, women against women lifetime abstainers: mortality RR 4.9 (4.0–6.2) at 24 g a day and 12.5 (8.8–17.7) at 60 g; morbidity 3.2 (2.6–3.9) and 6.2 (4.4–8.7). For men the text states only a similar, less pronounced pattern; men's values appear only as curves in Figure 2.

anchors.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph (starts p. 437; Danish figures on p. 438) and 3rd paragraph (p. 438)
anchors.extracted: Background cited by the authors, second-hand: a Danish study (ref. 10) found 27-fold (men) and 35-fold (women) mortality from alcoholic cirrhosis above five drinks (60 g) a day compared with the Danish general population; an Australian report (ref. 8) found more than ninefold risk above 40 g a day in both sexes, i.e. no sex difference in RR at heavy intake, though risks differed at 20–40 g.

The abstract states that the same average amount went with a higher risk of cirrhosis in women than in men; the results behind it are relative risks against same-sex lifetime abstainers (Table 2), as the claim correctly says.

reporting_issues.note: The substance is right, but the detail about Table 1 is not: Table 1's Sex column marks ten studies 'Both' without separating the seven with results by sex from the three without; those three are named in the text (refs 30, 36, 40: Klatsky 1981, Corrao 1991, Bellentani 1997; Results › Characteristics of the included studies, p. 440). What the paper does not say is whether the two Danish cohorts with end-point 'Both' (refs 39, 44) reported mortality and morbidity separately or combined. Consequence unchanged.
Table 2: interaction P = 0.05 for men at >0–12 g; text p. 441, 4th paragraph.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2, critically low: on my reading too, six of the seven critical items are not met (2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 13) and item 15 is met; items 8 and 16 'no' are right under the strict wording (no per-study exposure or comparator; no conflict-of-interest statement).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract's 'higher risk in women' (relative risks against same-sex abstainers, untested), the 'confirmed' mortality–morbidity hypothesis from between-study contrasts, and the omission of the men's significantly lower morbidity risks from the abstract.

missed: Sex comparison (Table 2, p. 442): the women's and men's 95% CIs do not overlap in 8 of 12 cells (all five mortality levels above 12 g a day; morbidity >12–24, >24–36 and >48–60 g), editors' comparison. Key finding 9 records only that no test was done. This bears on cl_alc_cirrhosis_women_men, which says the intervals overlap at most levels.
Table 2 gives no number of studies, datasets or cases behind any cell (p. 442); the card notes this only for the morbidity estimates (analysis.power).

Introduction background on sex, second-hand (pp. 437–438): an Australian report (ref. 8) found more than ninefold risk above 40 g a day in both sexes, i.e. no sex difference at heavy intake; a Danish study (ref. 10) found 27-fold (men) and 35-fold (women) cirrhosis mortality above 60 g a day against the Danish general population.

Wording slip (p. 439, Data extraction, 1st paragraph): the sick-quitter effect is said to raise lifetime abstainers' risk, whereas it is the abstainer group that includes former drinkers whose risk is raised; no effect on the estimates.
